beats.narration: Ranking rappers is useless, but it's also really fun. Every rap fan has a list. It's basically our national pastime at this point. And no argument on any of those lists has lasted longer, or gotten louder, than this one: Jay-Z or Drake.
beats.section: PART 1 — THE DEBATE THAT NEVER ENDS

beats.narration: They're not even enemies. They've made records together. Drake has two songs with Jay-Z on them, "Talk Up" and "Love All," and together they've done more than 359 million streams. But the second you put their names side by side, people pick a team.
beats.section: PART 1 — THE DEBATE THAT NEVER ENDS

beats.narration: And it should be easy. Rap keeps score better than almost any art form. Charts, plaques, streams, number ones: the numbers are public, and they go back decades. You'd think comparing two careers would be a simple task. But every time someone tries to settle it, the answer gets thrown out. Jay-Z fans say streaming rigged the numbers. Drake fans say the numbers are the numbers. Make the wrong argument, and the whole comment section dismisses you.
beats.section: PART 1 — THE DEBATE THAT NEVER ENDS

beats.narration: The arguments never change. Jay-Z fans point to the classic albums, the longevity, the business empire, the fact that he did it first. Drake fans point to the hits, the streams, the fact that for more than a decade, he has simply been everywhere. Both sides are sure they're right. Both sides have numbers. And somehow, both sides walk away from every argument more convinced than when they started.
beats.section: PART 1 — THE DEBATE THAT NEVER ENDS

beats.narration: So why is it so hard to settle a debate we have this much data on? Is it even possible to settle it at all? And if it is, how would we even do it?
beats.section: PART 1 — THE DEBATE THAT NEVER ENDS

beats.narration: The most popular approach is the formula. Build a point system. Give points for number one albums, points for number one singles, points for plaques, points for streams. Add it all up, and whoever has more points wins. It feels objective. It's just math.

But watch what happens when you change one rule. Count every album that went to number one on the Billboard 200, including collaborations and mixtapes, and Drake leads, 15 to 14. Count only studio albums, and Jay-Z leads, 11 to 9. Same charts, same two careers. Change one definition, and the winner changes.

That's the flaw in every formula. Somebody has to decide what a number one album is worth next to a number one single. Somebody has to decide whether a mixtape counts. Somebody has to decide if a plaque from 1998 is worth the same as a plaque from 2018. Every one of those decisions is an opinion. Pick the weights, and you've already picked the winner.

And people do pick them, usually without noticing. If you grew up buying albums, a number one album feels like the ultimate achievement, and singles feel like a bonus. If you grew up on playlists, a song that runs the world for a whole summer feels like the ultimate achievement, and albums feel like a container for singles. Neither of those instincts is wrong. But each one quietly writes a formula, and each formula already knows who it wants to win.
So let's remove the opinion. No weights, no formula, no definitions to argue about. Just the raw numbers, side by side.

On Spotify, Drake has 140 billion career streams. Jay-Z has 24.8 billion. Every single day, Drake pulls 58.5 million streams. Jay-Z pulls 10.7 million. That's more than five to one, and it's the same gap whether you look at the whole career or a single day.
The RIAA has certified 567.7 million units for Drake, across 168 certifications. For Jay-Z, it's 141 million, across 73. Four to one.

On the Hot 100, Drake has 404 entries. Jay-Z has 111. Drake has 92 top tens. Jay-Z has 23. Drake has 15 number ones, and 11 of them are his own singles. Jay-Z has 4. Only one of those, "Empire State of Mind," is his own single. The other three are Mariah Carey, Beyoncé and Rihanna records he's featured on.
In 2018 alone, Drake had four number one songs. That's as many as Jay-Z has had in his entire career.
And songs past a billion streams: Drake has 30. Jay-Z has 5.
That looks like the end of the debate. But raw numbers get weird fast.
beats.section: PART 4 — WHERE THE NUMBERS GET WEIRD

beats.narration: Out of the 31 artists we measured, Jay-Z ranks 13th in career streams. He's behind Drake, sure. He's also behind 21 Savage, Lil Baby and Metro Boomin. Almost nobody would argue that Metro Boomin has had the bigger career.
beats.section: PART 4 — WHERE THE NUMBERS GET WEIRD

beats.narration: Jay-Z's most-streamed song isn't even his. It's Rihanna's "Umbrella," at 2.37 billion. In fact, 45% of all of Jay-Z's streams come from songs where he's the featured artist. For Drake, it's 31%.
beats.section: PART 4 — WHERE THE NUMBERS GET WEIRD

beats.narration: And look at how the streams are spread. Jay-Z's five biggest songs make up 37% of his entire catalog's streams. Drake's five biggest make up less than 10% of his. Drake's catalog averages 253 million streams per track. Jay-Z's averages 55 million. Drake isn't living off a few hits. Everything he puts out gets played.
beats.section: PART 4 — WHERE THE NUMBERS GET WEIRD

beats.narration: None of these numbers are wrong. They're just answering a different question. Not who had the greater career, but who gets played the most right now. And by that measure, the answer was never in doubt.
beats.section: PART 4 — WHERE THE NUMBERS GET WEIRD

beats.narration: But there's one count where the gap closes: number one albums.
beats.section: PART 5 — THE ONE NUMBER THAT HOLDS

beats.narration: Look at how Jay-Z got there. His first two albums missed. Reasonable Doubt peaked at 23. In My Lifetime peaked at 3. Then, starting in 1998, every studio album he released went to number one. Hard Knock Life, the Blueprint, the Black Album, Kingdom Come, American Gangster, all the way through 4:44 in 2017. Eleven in a row, over nineteen years. He never missed again.
beats.section: PART 5 — THE ONE NUMBER THAT HOLDS

beats.narration: Nine of Drake's studio albums went to number one. But in 2026, two of them didn't. Maid of Honour peaked at three, and Habibti peaked at two.
beats.section: PART 5 — THE ONE NUMBER THAT HOLDS

beats.narration: The same thing shows up in certifications. Split the RIAA units by format, and Drake's singles have been certified for 509 million units against Jay-Z's 92.5 million. That's five and a half to one. But his albums? 58.5 million against Jay-Z's 47.5 million. On albums, it's close.
beats.section: PART 5 — THE ONE NUMBER THAT HOLDS

beats.narration: Why does this one lens hold when every other one collapses? Because a chart position isn't a total. It's a rank against everything else released that week. It doesn't care how big the market was, how many people had a phone in their pocket, or how many plays a song could rack up. It only asks one thing: in your moment, were you on top?
beats.section: PART 5 — THE ONE NUMBER THAT HOLDS

beats.narration: But "close" hides how they got there. Jay-Z's album total is built on depth. The RIAA has certified eighteen different Jay-Z albums. For Drake, it's fourteen.

Drake's is built on height. Jay-Z's biggest album, Hard Knock Life, is six-times platinum. Drake has four albums certified higher than that: Take Care, Views, Scorpion and Nothing Was the Same. Take Care is Diamond, ten million units. Jay-Z has never had a Diamond album.

And when you look at every record either of them has ever been on, the height gap gets even wider. Seventeen different Drake records have been certified Diamond. Jay-Z has two, "Empire State of Mind" and "Ni**as in Paris," and he shares both of them.
So even inside the one lens where Jay-Z holds level, it depends on how you look. Count the albums, and Jay-Z has more. Count the giants, and it's all Drake.
So should we just give Jay-Z's numbers an era bonus and call it even? That's what a lot of fans argue. Streaming inflated everything, so the old numbers should count for more.

But the data doesn't make that easy either. 82% of all of Jay-Z's certified units were certified in 2016 or later. Hard Knock Life, an album from 1998, reached six-times platinum in 2023. Streaming isn't just a Drake advantage. It's still counting votes for Jay-Z, decades after the records came out. So if you add an era bonus, how big is it? When does it stop applying? Every answer is another opinion.
There's another way to see these two careers: not as rivals, but as a handoff.

Jay-Z's last number one song came in 2009, with "Empire State of Mind." Drake's first came the very next year, in 2010, on Rihanna's "What's My Name?" One career's run at the top of the Hot 100 ends, and the other's begins.

From 2010 to 2017, when both of them were still releasing albums, Drake had seven number one albums. Jay-Z had three. But Jay-Z was already fourteen years past his debut album by then. Drake was just getting started.

And look at when each of them got recognized. Drake's busiest year for certifications was 2018, with 50 in a single year, and the typical record certified that year had come out in 2015. Jay-Z's busiest year was 2023, with 25, and the typical record certified that year had come out in 2009, fourteen years earlier. One of them gets certified while the records are still new. The other keeps getting certified long after.
So which question are we actually asking? Who was bigger, or who was greater?
beats.section: PART 9 — WHAT DO WE EVEN VALUE?

beats.narration: One fan ranks by totals: the most streams, the most plaques, the most number ones. Another fan ranks by how completely you ruled your own era. Both are reasonable. And they lead to different answers.
beats.section: PART 9 — WHAT DO WE EVEN VALUE?

beats.narration: So how do you settle a debate when people can't even agree on what matters?
beats.section: PART 9 — WHAT DO WE EVEN VALUE?

beats.narration: There's one method that has been proven to settle questions people can't agree on. Have you ever seen Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?

It was a game show where one contestant answered harder and harder multiple choice questions, all the way to the million-dollar question. When they got stuck, they had lifelines. The 50/50 removed two wrong answers. Phone a friend let them call someone for help, and it got them to the right answer about 66% of the time. And then there was ask the audience, where everyone in the studio voted. Ask the audience got the right answer 92% of the time. By far the most accurate lifeline the show ever had.

Think about that. The friend was usually someone the contestant picked because they were smart, someone they trusted. One informed person. The audience was a room full of strangers, most of whom had no special knowledge at all. And the strangers won, by a mile.

That's a concept called the wisdom of the crowd. The combined judgment of a large group is often more accurate than any one person in it, even an expert. Not because any individual in the crowd is especially smart, but because when you add up enough independent answers, the mistakes start pulling in different directions.

In 2011, the BBC put this to the test. They filled a jar with jelly beans and asked 160 people to guess how many were inside. The guesses were all over the place, from 500 to 50,000. Some people were wildly off.
The real number was 4,510. The average of all 160 guesses was 4,515. Off by five.
Every individual guess carried its own error and its own bias. But add enough of them together, and the errors cancel each other out. What's left is very close to the truth.
And here's the thing. In music, the crowd has already voted. It's been voting the entire time.
beats.section: PART 12 — THE CROWD HAS ALREADY VOTED

beats.narration: Every stream is a vote. Every album bought, every song played, every certification is millions of people answering the same question: what do I want to hear? Some of those votes come from casual listeners, some from superfans, some from people who just left a playlist running. Individually, every one of them is biased. A Drake fan replays the new album forty times. A Jay-Z fan plays the Black Album once a year on a road trip. Somebody hears "Umbrella" in a grocery store and adds it to a playlist without ever knowing Jay-Z is on it. Every single one of those votes is weird on its own. Together, they cancel out, just like the jelly beans.
beats.section: PART 12 — THE CROWD HAS ALREADY VOTED

beats.narration: And on that vote, it isn't close. 140 billion streams to 24.8. 567.7 million certified units to 141. Fifteen number one songs to four. Drake's 140 billion streams are more than any other artist we measured. The next closest, The Weeknd, has 97.2 billion.
beats.section: PART 12 — THE CROWD HAS ALREADY VOTED

beats.narration: But a crowd only votes in its own time. The crowd that showed up for Jay-Z showed up for albums, and it sent eleven straight studio albums to number one. The crowd of the streaming era showed up for everything, and it gave Drake numbers nobody else in our data comes close to.
beats.section: PART 12 — THE CROWD HAS ALREADY VOTED

beats.narration: So can we settle it? On the numbers, yes.
Drake dominated Jay-Z on every count but one. Streams, plaques, Hot 100 entries, top tens, number one songs, billion-stream records: Drake, by four or five to one.
The only lens where Jay-Z holds level is the one that ranks you against your own era: number one albums. And there, once his streak started, it was never broken.

That's not a knock on Jay-Z. Eleven straight number one studio albums across nineteen years is one of the most consistent runs any rapper has ever put together, and nothing in Drake's numbers erases it. But the debate was never really about whether Jay-Z was great. It was about who dominated, and the crowd has been answering that question every day for more than a decade.
Drake is the bigger artist. That isn't an opinion. It's what the crowd voted, billions of times over. Whether bigger makes him the greater one depends on which crowd you ask.
